= A tale of nefarious usage: IPv6 based Covert Channels =

Like steganographic techniques which uses unstructured data such as images, videos and audio to hide a message, network based covert channels uses the structure of the communication protocol itself to hide a message in plain sight hijacking legitimate communications providing a efficient and stelthy way to communicate and exfiltrate data.

The rapid adoption of IPv6, led by large Internet Service Providers, and technology companies, together with improvements will bring new security risks to be covered and addressed. One of those risks is represented by the possibility to easy implement covert channels over IPv6 based communications while remaining undetected by common open source IDPs like Suricata, Zeek and Snort. 

I present how by using high level programming language such Python and powerful open-source libraries like Scapy  is possible to hijack legitimate IPv6 traffic between two hosts by injecting covert data in one or more fields of the IPv6 packet without interrupting or deteriorating the overall communication at application level. This technique is not only usable on on-premises environments but also in hybrid-cloud and commercial cloud environments such as AWS, Azure and Vultr using an IPv6 network stack.

Six different covert channels have been implemented and tested in virtual and cloud environments to understand their feasibility and usability in the wild. In order to not disturb the legit communication the packets containing covert data are being cleaned before the delivery and all the injected data is removed restoring the packet to its original form. 

The Flow Label and Traffic Class fields, with the addition of Authentication, Routing Destination Option and Fragment extension headers can be exploited to reliably carry covert messages without affecting the overt communication. The bandwidth of the covert channel really depends on the amount of bits that can be safely exploited for a given field or extension header, for example the bandwidth of a covert channel exploiting the flow label is 20bits per packet and represent an efficient approach easy to implement and difficult to spot when high bandwidth is not required. On the other hand the implementation of a covert channel which exploits the Authentication Header, firstly implemented in this work, can inject 32bits per packet, while being really difficult to spot. Another great example is represented by the Destination Options Header, which usage is not really common, but if exploited allows to carry up to 256bits per packet.

To ensure the correct delivery of the covert channel and of the legit communication exploited to carry the hidden message a communication strategy must be applied to both ends of the covert communication to be sure to clean the affected package and to properly retrieve the bits belonging to the hidden message. The three communication strategies implemented are: naive, marked and reliable. Characterized by an increased level of complexity and greater reliability or efficiency. "Naive" strategy consists in simply sending a burst of n packets containing a covert followed by y legit packets; both the sender and the receiver are configured with the same n and y parameters. Of course this strategy is not fully reliable in case of packet loss or in situations in which the order of delivery is not ensured. For this reason the marked strategy implements a cryptographic marking of each packet containing covert data ensuring that that the receiver correctly know how many packets and the order in which they should be assembled. The reliable communication strategy can be applied only when the exploited legit communication uses TCP at level 6, allowing the sender to check if the current TCP sequence number is lower than the expected TCP sequence number the covert bits associated with the specific TCP sequence number will be re-transmitted. 

In addition to works already present in the academic literature the tool I propose allows the possibility to perform a man-in-the-middle data exfiltration allowing a compromised router to be part of the attack chain. In combination with an evaluation of covert channels performance measured in bandwidth and ratio of loss messages over correctly delivered messages their implementation has been tested against a set of open-source available IDS: Surica, Snort and Zeek in order to understand if the common detection rules trigger any detection when scanning IPv6 traffic hijacked to carry a covert packet.
